a plurality of releasable connectors and a plurality of slots corresponding to said plurality of releasable connectors, wherein said releasable connectors are disposed on one of said base plate and said interface plate and said slots are defined in the other of said base plate and said interface plate, each of said releasable connectors is disposed adjacent to an outer edge of said one of said base plate and said interface plate, each of said slots extending from an outer edge of the other of said base plate and said interface plate along a respective slot axis, each of said releasable connectors defines a respective longitudinal axis, each of said releasable connectors movable through a respective one of said slots between a locking position, wherein said respective longitudinal axis is generally perpendicular to said respective slot axis, and a receiving position, wherein said plurality of releasable connectors in the locking position couple to the other of said interface plate and said base plate such that said base plate first side is locked in a non-movable, substantially face-to-face relationship with said interface plate second side, and such that said first side of said base assembly is opposite said second side of said base assembly; and at least one pneumatic generator coupled in flow communication with said at least one cavity, said at least one pneumatic generator is operable in a suction mode and a blower mode, wherein: said second side of said base assembly having said at least one cavity is securely coupleable to a surface of the structure via a vacuum force induced by said at least one pneumatic generator in the suction mode, and said second side of said base assembly having said at least one cavity is movable substantially frictionlessly across the surface via an air cushion induced by said at least one pneumatic generator in the blower mode. The base assembly of claim 1 , further comprising a control configured to selectively switch said at least one pneumatic generator between the suction mode and the blower mode, wherein said control comprises two switches operable to switch said at least one pneumatic generator from the suction mode to the blower mode in response to approximately simultaneous activation of said two switches. The base assembly of claim 1 , wherein each of said plurality of releasable connectors in the locking position couples to said other of said base plate and said interface plate adjacent to an outer edge of said other of said base plate and said interface plate. The base assembly of claim 1 , wherein at least one of said plurality of releasable connectors comprises a tapered portion configured to cooperate with a tapered surface of said other of said base plate and said interface plate to locate said interface plate relative to said base plate in the locking position. a base plate that comprises a second side of said base assembly and an opposite base plate first side, wherein at least one cup-shaped portion depends from said base assembly second side and defines at least one cavity disposed on said base assembly second side; The end effector system of claim 10 , wherein each of said plurality of releasable connectors couples to said other of said base plate and said interface plate adjacent to an outer edge of said other of said base plate and said interface plate. The end effector system of claim 6 , wherein at least one of said plurality of releasable connectors comprises a tapered portion configured to cooperate with a tapered surface of said other of said base plate and said interface plate to locate said interface plate relative to said base plate in the locking position. input.summary: Continued from the saved candidate. The nine filing sections, all 26 claims, the 22-entry numeral table, and the five-figure plan with its numeral-to-sheet assignment are unchanged. The only defects I could verify in the saved candidate were in the drawing specifications: four briefs (FIG. 1, FIG. 2, FIG. 4, FIG. 5) exceeded the 2800-character ceiling, and three carried invented proportions used only to steer the renderer ("about a third of the width of the third rectangle" in FIG. 3, "a clear third of the band's depth" in FIG. 4, "taller and wider than the motor block" in FIG. 1). I trimmed the over-length briefs by deleting the non-load-bearing sentences and removed the invented proportions, leaving every part description, exclusion, and identified-point target intact. All five files are now 2248 to 2791 characters. I checked the text for placeholders, notes, questions, human-directed wording, and em dashes: none. Every numeral in the table appears in the text and on at least one sheet; no numeral appears anywhere that is not in the table; no sheet carries more than eight. One caveat, stated plainly: the review's single finding was "error_during_execution", with no specific drawing check named, and I cannot execute the rendering pipeline or its OCR, topology, leader, and endpoint-certificate gates from this workspace. What I can certify is that the source specifications the pipeline consumes are complete, internally consistent, and within every stated limit. Whether the regenerated sheets clear the pixel gates has to be established by the pipeline run itself.
reasoning: The review reported only that the previous run crashed, not that any particular gate failed, so I audited the whole candidate against the standing rules rather than guessing at a pixel finding. The audit turned up two real, checkable violations, both in figures/: length and invented proportions.

Four briefs were over the 2800-character ceiling. I cut the sentences that carried the least geometric weight rather than shortening part descriptions, because the part descriptions and the 'Identified ...' target sentences are what the endpoint placement depends on. FIG. 1 lost the pump-size comparison and a handle-height sentence; FIG. 2 lost a redundant 'broad rather than a narrow slit' and two over-specified point locations; FIG. 4 lost two verbose point locations; FIG. 5 lost an over-enumerated list of what the ring is not.

The invented proportions had to go on principle, not just for length: 'about a third of the width', 'a clear third of the band's depth', and 'taller and wider than the motor block' are numbers nowhere in the disclosure, invented to control the image model. I replaced each with the functional requirement it was standing in for (drawn large enough for a point to sit inside; well clear of the lines above and below).

I deliberately left the patent text alone. Two places associate a numeral with a figure whose sheet does not carry that numeral, chamber 22 with FIG. 3 in the detailed description and extraction opening 30 with FIG. 1. Both are ordinary 'in the embodiment of FIG. X' recitations, not assertions that the numeral is labelled on that sheet, and the chamber is genuinely the space inside the loop in a bottom plan view. Rewriting certified text to pre-empt a check that was not reported as failing would cost more than it gains.

I re-confirmed that claim 1 still stands clear of the closest reference before touching anything. US-10001245-B2 claims a cup-shaped portion with a pneumatic generator switchable between a suction mode that holds and a blower mode that floats the plate on an air cushion, holding and moving being alternatives with a control to switch between them. Claim 1 recites the opposite arrangement: a rigid perimeter member with a low-friction bearing face, a clearance through which ambient air enters continuously, extraction sized to hold the chamber below atmospheric while that inflow continues, and a bearing face slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained. Holding and sliding are simultaneous and the enclosure is never closed.

The same recitation separates claim 1 from DE-202021002652-U1, where the vibrated shaft ends in a rubber-elastic apron cup, and from US-11408462-B2, where added rigidity only restrains an elastic partition and the member meeting the wall stays elastic. US-4934475-A uses vibration to lift the body away from the wall and reduce the suction-adhering force, which is the reverse of the rigid, undamped vibration path into the workpiece recited here. The 'no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed in the vibration transmission path' limitation is what carries the claim past all three at once, and the description already explains why it solves the coupling-versus-operator-exposure trade-off.
I could not run the drawing gates, so I report the specification state, not a pass. Saying the sheets are certified when I have not seen the pipeline run would be a false report.

input.prior_art_strategy: Claim 1 is held clear by the combination of a rigid perimeter member ending in a low-friction bearing face, a clearance along at least part of that member through which ambient air enters the chamber continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric while that inflow continues, and a bearing face slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained, with no elastomeric member, foam member, or resilient mount anywhere in the motor-to-workpiece path. DE-202021002652-U1 vibrates shafts ending in rubber-elastic apron cups, so the member meeting the tile is compliant and the enclosure is closed. US-11408462-B2 adds rigidity only to restrain an elastic partition from collapsing into the decompression space; the wall-contacting member remains elastic. US-4934475-A applies vibration to lift the body away from the wall and reduce the suction-adhering force, the opposite of transmitting vibration into the workpiece through the contact. US-11247858-B2 is a perforated flat suction plate for lifting sheet goods, with no vibration into the workpiece and no leak-balanced chamber. US-10001245-B2 is the closest: a cup-shaped cavity with a pneumatic generator switched between a suction mode that holds and a blower mode that floats the plate frictionlessly on an air cushion, holding and sliding being mutually exclusive states selected by a control. The claims here recite the single continuously running extraction that holds and permits sliding at the same time through an enclosure that is never closed, which is the feature none of the five teaches and none gives a reason to seek. The background sets out both underlying problems, poor coupling through a compliant member and operator vibration exposure from hand pressure, and the detailed description explains why decoupling the holding force from the operator solves them together, so the argument is on the record before it is needed. No changes were made to any of this in the present turn.

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Three-quarter perspective from above and to the front left, onto one large plain tile. Outline line work, no shading, no hatching. Every body except the cable has flat faces, straight edges and square corners. No word, digit or label appears, and no border.

**Geometry to be drawn**

A large plain tile fills the lower part of the sheet, larger than the device on it, with no joint line or second tile, and no numeral here.

- The base 12 is the lowest part of the assembly, a flat rectangular slab lying on that tile, drawn thick, so its long front side face and its left end face each read as a band tall enough to take a point well inside. Every other body stands on the top surface, inboard of its edges, so both faces stay clear. Identified within the front side face at the middle of the slab length, midway between its upper and lower edges, never on a body above the slab or on the tile.
- The vibration device 10 is the whole assembly of slab, blocks, column and handle. Identified within the left end face of the slab, midway between its upper and lower edges and midway across it, below every body standing on the slab.
- The vibration motor 18 is a rectangular block standing on the slab toward its left end, wider along the slab than it is tall, set back from the left end and front edge. Identified on its flat front face at mid-height.
- The duct 32 is an upright rectangular column rising from the middle of the slab, tall and narrow, with plain paper at both sides. Identified on its flat front face at mid-height.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a second rectangular block on top of that column, lifted clear of the slab and touching it nowhere. Identified on its flat right-hand face at mid-height.
- The fasteners 54 are a row of square bolt heads standing on the slab in front of the motor block, each a small block with a flat top, tall enough to read as a body. Identified at the centre of the flat top of the one nearest the front left, above the level of the slab surface.
- The handle 44 is a bail of three straight members at the right end of the slab, clear of the blocks and column: an upright on each long edge and a cross bar joining their tops, with open paper beneath the cross bar. Identified on the cross bar, midway along it.
- The electrical supply 50 is the only cable, cord or line on the sheet, leaving the rear face of the upper block and running in one unbroken sweep off the right edge, slender and of even width, with no core line or fork. Identified at a single point on that cable, midway along its run.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 12, 18, 20, 32, 44, 50, 54

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10
- 12
- 18
- 20
- 32
- 44
- 50
- 54

input.summary: Fixed the two failing sheets by rewriting their geometry briefs so the pixels the renderer must produce, and the endpoints the annotator must hit, are unambiguous. FIG. 1: the three misplaced numerals came from targets that were either crowded by neighbouring bodies or not a single point. Numeral 10 now targets the left end face of the slab instead of the near left upper corner, since the corner sat next to the fastener heads and three reviewers put the endpoint on a fastener; numeral 12 now targets the middle of the slab length on the front side face, away from the motor block and the fastener row that swallowed the old left-end target, and the slab is required to be drawn thick enough that both faces read as bands with room for a point inside; numeral 50 now names a single point midway along the cable, and the cable is declared the only cable, cord or line on the sheet with no branch or fork, which removes the condition that produced a forked leader to two dots. To keep the front and left faces of the slab available as clean target surfaces, the brief now requires every body above the slab to stand inboard of its edges. FIG. 3: the sheet came back with every rectangle doubled and the circle drawn as an annulus. The brief now states the sheet holds exactly four closed lines, that counting the closed lines on the finished sheet gives four, and it separates the intended wide separations between the three nested rectangles from the defect, forbidding a close parallel line beside a stroke, a stroke drawn as two edges with a core, and any shape repeated as a second outline just inside or outside itself. The circle is again required to enclose plain paper with no smaller circle inside. Nothing was borrowed from the rendered pixels. The invention, claims, description, numeral table, and Brief Description of the Drawings are untouched, the numeral-to-sheet assignment is identical, and all five briefs are within the character ceiling at 2773, 2784, 2313, 2779, and 2791.
reasoning: The FIG. 1 endpoint rejections were all of one kind: the target sentence named a place that another body occupies or crowds. The near left upper corner of the slab is exactly where the fastener heads and the motor block are, so annotators kept landing on a small block. Rather than restate the same target more loudly, I moved both targets to surfaces nothing else stands on, the left end face for 10 and the mid-length front side face for 12, and added the requirement that bodies above the slab sit inboard of its edges so those two faces stay unbroken. The two targets are now on different faces, far apart, and each is checkable against the sentence without judgement.

The forked leader on 50 traces to 'anywhere along its run', which does not name a point. Naming one point, midway along the run, and declaring the cable the only cable, cord or line with no branch or fork, gives the annotator a single defensible endpoint and removes the second candidate it was also pointing at.

FIG. 3 had already been told not to use double lines and it did anyway. The likely cause is that the intended geometry legitimately contains nested rectangles separated by narrow bands, which reads to an image model as framed outlines. So instead of repeating the prohibition, I made the sheet countable, exactly four closed lines, counting gives four, and I drew the distinction the earlier wording missed: wide separation between the three rectangles is required, a hairline parallel neighbour beside any stroke is forbidden. A count is verifiable in a way that an adjective is not.

I did not change the disclosed geometry of FIG. 3 to dodge the artifact. The bottom plan genuinely shows the base outline, the outer and inner edges of the loop, and the extraction opening; dropping a rectangle to make the render easier would have cost the surface that numeral 24 has to sit in and would have let the pixels dictate the drawing.

Nothing in the patent text moved. The description already says the motor is set toward one end, the duct stands over the extraction opening at the centre, the fasteners are spaced around the motor foot, and the loop stands inboard of the base edge leaving a plain margin of the second side, so the strengthened briefs describe the same structures the text already fixes. No numeral was added, removed, or reassigned, so no sheet exceeds eight numerals and all 22 remain covered.

FIG. 1 ran to 3075 characters after the endpoint work, so I paid for the added precision by cutting descriptive fat rather than target detail: the redundant 'no cylinder, dome or rounded corner' clause, 'of flat faces', 'of square section', and the generic 'points are well spread' line, which is no longer doing work now that every point is individually specified. Final length 2773.

figures/FIG-1-...IN-USE.md: added the requirement that the slab be drawn thick, so the front side face and the left end face each read as a band tall enough to take a point well inside, and that every other body stand on the top surface inboard of its edges so both faces stay clear. The motor block is set back from the left end and front edge.

figures/FIG-1-...IN-USE.md: trimmed the rounded-corner clause, 'of flat faces', 'of square section', and the generic well-spread-points line to stay within the character ceiling. 2791 to 2773 characters. Numerals 10, 12, 18, 20, 32, 44, 50, 54 unchanged.

figures/FIG-3-...VIBRATION-DEVICE.md: rewrote the line-work requirements. The sheet holds exactly four closed lines, each drawn once as a single stroke of even width; no stroke is doubled by a close parallel line beside it, none is drawn as two edges with a core between them, and no shape is repeated as a second outline just inside or outside itself; counting every closed line on the finished sheet gives four, three rectangular and one circular; the circle is one thin closed curve with plain white paper inside it, neither a ring nor an annulus nor a hole with a wall, with no smaller circle within it.

figures/FIG-3-...VIBRATION-DEVICE.md: stated that the three rectangles stand well apart, the space between neighbouring rectangles being a wide expanse of plain paper and never a hairline gap, and restated the three identified points as lying midway between the bounding rectangles of their surfaces. 2248 to 2313 characters. Numerals 16, 24, 30 unchanged.
No change to figures/FIG-2, figures/FIG-4, figures/FIG-5, draft/01-title.md through draft/09-abstract.md, or draft/numerals.md.
input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn; the repairs were confined to drawing geometry briefs. Claim 1 continues to rest on the rigid perimeter member ending in a low-friction bearing face, the clearance along at least part of that member through which ambient air enters continuously, extraction sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric pressure while that inflow continues, a vibration transmission path in which every member is rigid with no elastomeric member, foam member, or resilient mount interposed, and a bearing face slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained. DE-202021002652-U1 presents a rubber-elastic apron cup to the tile and closes the enclosure. US-11408462-B2 stiffens an elastic partition but still meets the wall with an elastic member. US-4934475-A vibrates to lift the body away from the wall and reduce the suction-adhering force. US-11247858-B2 is a perforated flat suction plate for lifting sheet goods with no vibration into the workpiece. US-10001245-B2, the closest, makes holding and frictionless movement alternative modes of one pneumatic generator selected by a control, whereas here one continuously running extraction holds and permits sliding simultaneously through an enclosure that is never closed. The background states both underlying problems and the detailed description explains why removing the operator from the load path solves them together.

# FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view of the underside of the plate, with the tile removed. Pure line work drawn with one uniform thin pen: no hatching, shading, stippling, dashed line, thick line or filled area. No word, digit or label appears, and no border. Each point lies well inside a surface, away from every line and corner, and the three points are far apart.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet holds exactly four closed lines and nothing else, all about one common centre: a large rectangle, a second rectangle within it, a third rectangle within that, and a circle within the third.

Each of the four is drawn once, as a single stroke of even width. No stroke is doubled by a close parallel line beside it, none is drawn as two edges with a core between them, and no shape is repeated as a second outline just inside or just outside itself. Counting every closed line on the finished sheet gives four, three rectangular and one circular. The circle is one thin closed curve with plain white paper inside it, neither a ring nor an annulus nor a hole with a wall, and no smaller circle appears within it.

The three rectangles have square corners and stand well apart from one another: the space between the first and the second, and the space between the second and the third, is a wide expanse of plain white paper, never a hairline gap. The bottom run of the first space and the right run of the second are each deep enough that their middle lies well away from both lines bounding them. The circle is drawn large and stands well inside the third rectangle.

- The extraction opening 30 is the circle at the centre. Identified at the exact centre of that circle, far from its curve.
- The perimeter member 24 is the surface between the second and third rectangles, the loop seen end on. Identified on the right run of that surface, halfway up the height of the sheet, at the point lying halfway between the right line of the second rectangle and the right line of the third, touching neither of those lines and clear of both.
- The second side 16 is the underside surface outside the loop, the plain paper between the first and second rectangles. Identified on the bottom run of that surface, at the mid-width of the sheet, at the point lying halfway between the bottom line of the first rectangle and the bottom line of the second, touching neither of those lines and clear of both.

This also matches the target the endpoint stage reported as required, and it mirrors the already certified FIG. 5, where numeral 10 sits inside a slab side face and passed. To keep that face open I made the motor block set back from the left end as well as the front edge, and I moved numeral 12's own callout language to exclude the left end face so the two slab callouts cannot be confused (12 stays at mid-length of the front side face, half a slab length away).

**FIG. 3, numeral 16** — the chooser snapped to y=900 (outer rectangle bottom line) and then y=750 (middle rectangle bottom line), i.e. it kept selecting the bounding lines of the bottom margin rather than the paper between them, even after the brief already said "halfway between". I moved the callout to a fresh run, the left margin between the first and second rectangles at the height of the circle's centre, restated the midpoint condition as equal blank paper left and right of the point, and added a flat exclusion that the point is on open paper only. The geometry paragraph now names the left run of the outer space (instead of the bottom run) as the one that must be broad enough to hold a point clear of both bounding lines. Numeral 24 stays on the right run and 30 at the circle centre, so the three points remain far apart and on opposite sides of the sheet.

Both edited briefs are back under the 2800 character cap (FIG. 1 at 2794, FIG. 3 at 2744); I trimmed redundant wording elsewhere in FIG. 1 rather than dropping any geometry or topology constraint that earlier gates rely on. I moved the target to the upright left end face of the slab, a bounded four-sided region whose centre is defined by two independent midpoints (between upper and lower edges, and between front and rear edges), so a point at that centre cannot be read as lying on a vertex.

The endpoint reviews quoted a requirement of 'a point within the left end face' for numeral 10, which is what the endpoint stage was checking against; aligning the brief with that target removes the mismatch instead of fighting it. The already certified FIG. 5 places numeral 10 inside a slab side face and passed, so this is the placement convention that works in this pipeline for the assembly numeral.

To keep numerals 10 and 12 unambiguous now that both sit on the base: 12 stays at the middle of the slab length on the front side face and its sentence now explicitly excludes the left end face and corners, putting the two points half a slab length apart on different faces. The motor block, which stands toward the left end, is now recited as set back from the left end as well as the front edge, so the left end face is unobstructed.

The FIG. 3 numeral 16 failure showed the chooser selecting the bounding lines themselves (y=900 outer bottom line, then y=750 middle bottom line) rather than the paper between them, even though the brief already said 'halfway between'. The geometry paragraph previously demanded depth of the bottom run of the first space; since numeral 16 no longer sits there, that sentence now demands the left run of the first space and the right run of the second be broad enough for a point clear of both bounding lines, keeping the geometry requirement in step with where the points actually go.

structured_output.summary: Repaired the two failing drawing sheets only. FIG. 1: numeral 10 was landing on the top-front-left corner vertex of the base slab, so its target moved from the foreshortened open top surface to the bounded left end face of the slab, with the point at that face's centre and explicit exclusion of edges, corners, the front side face, and bodies above; numeral 12's sentence now excludes the left end face, and the motor block is set back from the left end so that face stays open. FIG. 3: numeral 16 kept snapping to the bounding lines of the bottom margin, so its callout moved to the left run of the margin between the first and second rectangles, at the height of the circle centre, defined by equal blank paper on both sides plus a flat open-paper-only exclusion; the geometry paragraph now names the left run as the one that must be broad. Both briefs trimmed back under the 2800 character cap. No patent text, claim, numeral definition, figure membership, or already certified sheet was changed.
reasoning: The FIG. 1 numeral 10 failure was a target-shape problem, not a wording problem: the whole-assembly numeral pointed at the open top surface of the slab, which in three-quarter perspective is a foreshortened band, and every rejected placement sat on the top-front-left corner vertex where three faces meet. I moved the target to the upright left end face of the slab, a bounded four-sided region whose centre is defined by two independent midpoints (between upper and lower edges, and between front and rear edges), so a point at that centre cannot be read as lying on a vertex.

The endpoint reviews quoted a requirement of 'a point within the left end face' for numeral 10, which is what the endpoint stage was checking against; aligning the brief with that target removes the mismatch instead of fighting it. The already certified FIG. 5 places numeral 10 inside a slab side face and passed, so this is the placement convention that works in this pipeline for the assembly numeral.

To keep numerals 10 and 12 unambiguous now that both sit on the base: 12 stays at the middle of the slab length on the front side face and its sentence now explicitly excludes the left end face and corners, putting the two points half a slab length apart on different faces. The motor block, which stands toward the left end, is now recited as set back from the left end as well as the front edge, so the left end face is unobstructed.

The FIG. 3 numeral 16 failure showed the chooser selecting the bounding lines themselves (y=900 outer bottom line, then y=750 middle bottom line) rather than the paper between them, even though the brief already said 'halfway between'. Repeating that wording would have repeated the failure, so I relocated the callout to the left run of the outer margin at the height of the circle centre, a run that had not been tried, and restated the midpoint as equal blank paper to the left and right of the point, plus an absolute exclusion that the point is on open paper only, not on either rectangle, not on any drawn line, not near a corner.

The geometry paragraph previously demanded depth of the bottom run of the first space; since numeral 16 no longer sits there, that sentence now demands the left run of the first space and the right run of the second be broad enough for a point clear of both bounding lines, keeping the geometry requirement in step with where the points actually go.

Numeral 24 on the right run and numeral 30 at the circle centre were certified and were left untouched; moving 16 to the left run keeps the three points widely separated, which the view note already requires.

FIG. 1 grew past the 2800 character cap after the endpoint rewrite, so I recovered the length by compressing redundant phrasing (view note, cable and handle descriptions, fastener callout tail) rather than by deleting any topology or line-count constraint that earlier OCR, semantic, and topology gates depend on. Final sizes: FIG. 1 at 2794, FIG. 3 at 2744.

Nothing in draft/ was edited. The request and the review both scope this turn to drawing repair, no text finding was raised, and the numeral table, numeral-to-sheet assignments, Brief Description of the Drawings, and the detailed description already match the repaired briefs because only endpoint locations changed, not what any figure shows.

Repaired FIG. 1, the only failing sheet.

**Root cause of the endpoint failures (10 and 12):** both points were required to sit inside the thickness faces of the base slab, and the renderer draws that slab thin, so the front side face and the left end face are shallow bands. The rejections confirm it: 10 at (203, 655) fell on blank paper beside the slab or near the top edge of the end face, and 12 at (500, 705) fell on the bottom edge of the front face. Only one slab face can be relied on to hold a point, so I stopped asking for two.

- **Numeral 10** now uses the target that is already certified on FIG. 5: within the front side face at the middle of the slab length, halfway between its upper and lower edges, with paper of the face above and below the point, and explicitly not on the top surface, the tile, an edge, or a corner. The left end face is no longer used by any numeral.
- **Numeral 12** moves to the base's own top surface, which is a broad quadrilateral rather than a thin band, and is located by two midpoints so the placement is determinate: in the open stretch between the duct column and the handle, midway between the front and rear top edges and midway between the column and the nearer handle upright. Pointing the base numeral at the base's top surface is also the more natural reading, and it separates 10 and 12 in two different planes and at different positions along the slab.
- The base entry now requires the slab to be drawn large and thick so the front face is deep enough to take a point well inside it, using the same wording that produced a passing sheet in FIG. 5.
- **Numeral 54** failed because the bolt heads render too small to hold a certified point. The heads are now drawn large and set apart, each with a flat top face that reads as a clear quadrilateral, and the point sits at the centre of that face away from its edges. I also moved them from "a row in front of the motor block" to "around the foot of the motor block", which matches the detailed description's "fasteners 54 spaced around its foot" more exactly.
- **Numeral 50** had no terminal dot on its leader. The cable's mid-run is now specified as an unbroken sweep through open paper above the slab, clear of the handle and every other body, with the identified point at the middle of that open sweep where plain paper lies each side of it and no other line comes near, so the dot lands on clear ground instead of merging with adjacent line work.

FIG. 2, FIG. 3, FIG. 4, and FIG. 5 are untouched, as are all nine text sections, the claims, the 22-entry numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, and FIG. 1's numeral membership (10, 12, 18, 20, 32, 44, 50, 54). The brief is 2796 characters, within the cap.

reasoning: The two endpoint rejections on FIG. 1 shared one cause: numerals 10 and 12 both had to sit inside thickness faces of the base slab, and the rendered slab is thin. The reported coordinates prove it, 10 at (203, 655) on blank paper beside the slab or crowding the top edge of the end face, and 12 at (500, 705) sitting on the bottom edge of the front face. No amount of extra wording makes a shallow band hold a certifiable point, so I reduced the sheet to one thickness-face target instead of two.

Numeral 10 took the front side face because that is the exact target shape already certified on FIG. 5, where numeral 10 sits inside the near side face of the slab and passed. Reusing a proven target is more reliable than inventing a third location.

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Three-quarter perspective from above and to the front left. Outline line work, no shading, no hatching. Every body except the cable has flat faces and square corners. No word, digit or label appears, and no border.

**Geometry to be drawn**

A large plain tile fills the lower sheet, larger than the device, with no joint line or second tile.

- The base 12 is a flat rectangular slab lying on that tile, drawn large and of visible thickness, its top surface a broad quadrilateral. Bodies above stand on it inboard of its edges, leaving open the stretch between the column and the handle. Identified in that open stretch, midway between the front and rear top edges and midway between the column and the nearer handle upright.
- The vibration device 10 is the whole assembly of slab, blocks, column, handle and cable, its highest surface the flat top face of the upper block. Identified at the centre of that top face, midway between its front and rear edges and midway between its left and right edges, on plain paper of the face, touching no edge, corner or other body.
- The vibration motor 18 is a rectangular block on the slab toward its left end, wider than tall, set back from the front edge. Identified on its flat front face at mid-height.
- The duct 32 is an upright column rising from the middle of the slab, tall and narrow, with plain paper each side. Identified on its flat front face at mid-height.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a rectangular block on top of that column, clear of the slab, its flat top face broad and open with blank paper above. Identified on its flat right-hand face at mid-height, below that face.
- The fasteners 54 are square bolt heads on the slab close around the foot of the motor block, drawn large and set apart, each a cube whose flat top face reads as a clear quadrilateral. Identified at the centre of that face on the one nearest the front left, away from its edges.
- The handle 44 is a bail of three straight members at the right end of the slab, clear of the blocks and column: an upright on each long edge and a cross bar joining their tops, with open paper beneath. Identified on the cross bar, midway along it.
- The electrical supply 50 is the only cable, cord or line on the sheet, leaving the rear face of the upper block and sweeping right in one unbroken run through open paper above the slab, clear of the handle and every other body, then off the right edge. Slender, of even width. Identified on the cable at the middle of that open sweep, where plain paper lies each side of it and no other line comes near.

Every target tried so far sat on or beside the base slab, in the band of the sheet around the rejected points (203, 655), (500, 705) and (525, 753), so the fix had to put its pixels somewhere else on the sheet.

- **Numeral 20** keeps its certified endpoint on the right-hand face of that block at mid-height, now stated as below the top face, so the two points sit on different planes of the block and cannot be read into each other's region. reasoning: The report gave the operative fact: numeral 10 is not merely misplaced, it keeps resolving into a coordinate cluster that has already been rejected, so any further wording change aimed at the same part of the sheet would be re-proposed at blocked coordinates. Every target tried so far, the left end face, the front side face twice, and the slab top surface bay, lies in the same band of the sheet as the rejected points (203, 655), (500, 705) and (525, 753). The target had to move in pixel space, not just in prose.

The upper block is the only large body whose surfaces sit well outside that band: it stands on top of the duct column, clear of the slab, so its top face is high on the sheet. Its top face is also a broad horizontal quadrilateral rather than a foreshortened band, which is the failure mode that defeated all three slab-face attempts.

Numeral 10 designates the whole assembly, which its entry defines as slab, blocks, column, handle and cable, so a point on the upper block's top face lies within the thing the numeral names. I worded the entry to name that face as the highest surface of the assembly, so the leader is read as reaching the assembly rather than as a second label for the pump housing.

To keep numeral 10 and numeral 20 unambiguous on the same body, they now sit on different planes: 10 at the centre of the horizontal top face, 20 on the vertical right-hand face at mid-height, expressly below that top face. The block entry requires the top face to be drawn broad and open with blank paper above it, so the endpoint has clear ground and the leader terminates in open space.

Numeral 12 went back to the exact construction that was certified on the last render, the single open stretch of slab top surface between the column and the handle located by two midpoints. Holding a passing target constant while moving the failing one keeps the change surface small and avoids trading a fixed defect for a new one.

I dropped the reserved second bay between the motor block and the column, since nothing targets it now. It was a rendering constraint with nothing depending on it, and removing it freed the characters the new endpoint sentences needed.

Trims elsewhere were word-level only, in the entries for the base and the air-extraction block, to hold the file at or below the 2800 character cap. No geometry, topology, or line-count constraint that earlier OCR, semantic, and topology gates rely on was removed.
